sources.news_title: Ministry Sets Deadline: Pentagon Pushes US Defense Industry to Increase Production
sources.text:
Ministerium setzt FristPentagon drängt US-Rüstungsindustrie zu mehr Produktion
Laut Experten schwinden die Waffenreserve der USA aufgrund des Iran-Kriegs. Das Verteidigungsministerium fordert von der heimischen Rüstungsindustrie nun eine rasche Steigerung der Produktion. In nur drei Wochen sollen die Unternehmen entsprechende Pläne vorlegen.
Das Pentagon hat Vertreter der US-Rüstungsindustrie dazu aufgefordert, die Produktion und Lieferung von Waffen rasch zu steigern. Das berichten die "Washington Post" und der US-Sender CNN übereinstimmend unter Berufung auf eine Mitteilung eines Ministeriumsvertreters. Pentagon-Sprecher Sean Parnell bestätigte die Echtheit des Dokuments. Es fällt in eine Zeit, in der Experten und Berichte von US-Medien zuletzt immer wieder auf schwindende Waffenreserven im US-Militär als Folge des Iran-Kriegs hingewiesen hatten. US-Präsident Donald Trump wies das zurück.
Der stellvertretende US-Verteidigungsminister Steve Feinberg habe Vertretern der Rüstungsindustrie am Mittwoch eine Frist von maximal drei Wochen übermittelt, um Pläne vorzulegen, die schnellere Liefertermine beziehungsweise eine gesteigerte Produktion für kritische Fähigkeiten vorsähen, zitieren CNN und die "Washington Post" aus dem Dokument. Laut der Zeitung soll Feinberg darin eine klare Erwartung geäußert haben: "Jahrelange Entwicklungszyklen sind nicht akzeptabel." Man müsse die Pläne drastisch beschleunigen und die Produktionskapazitäten jetzt ausbauen, zitiert ihn die "Washington Post" weiter.
Seit dem ersten Tag von Pete Hegseth als US-Verteidigungsminister konzentriere sich das Pentagon darauf, einen Wandel hinsichtlich der Geschwindigkeit, Kapazität und Schlagkraft der amerikanischen Verteidigungsindustrie herbeizuführen, betonte Parnell in einem Statement. Hegseths Stellvertreter Feinberg arbeite daran, ein veraltetes Beschaffungssystem zu reformieren. "Direkt mit führenden Vertretern der Industrie zusammenzuarbeiten, um die Produktion zu beschleunigen, ist nichts Neues."
Die Denkfabrik Center For Strategic & International Studies (CSIS) in Washington schätzte Stand Ende Juli, dass der USA noch bis zu knapp 830 Patriot-Abwehrraketen zur Verfügung stünden. Vor dem Iran-Krieg seien es geschätzt rund 2300 gewesen. Bei THAAD-Abwehrraketen ging die Denkfabrik von 452 vor dem Krieg aus. Ende Juli seien es geschätzt noch bis zu 278 Raketen gewesen.

sources.news_title: Pentagon seeks weapons production boost
sources.text:
The Pentagon’s No. 2 official asked major U.S. defense companies to accelerate efforts to produce and deliver key weapons systems amid new concerns about shortages and gaps exacerbated by the Iran war.
Steve Feinberg, the deputy secretary of defense, said the department is targeting accelerated or increased procurement for critical programs including wide-area surveillance, air-defense sensors and interceptors, and missile-tracking systems.
“Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,” he wrote in an Aug. 5 letter seen by Bloomberg to major defense companies, including Boeing Co., Lockheed Martin Corp. and RTX Corp. “We must dramatically accelerate our program schedules and expand our production capacity now.” The Washington Post reported earlier on the letter.
There have been growing warnings about the state of U.S. weapons stockpiles as the U.S. military attacks Iran and repels its drone and missile strikes on American bases in the region.
President Donald Trump has denied the U.S. is running low on munitions, saying on Thursday the country has “massive amounts” of them, while warning of punishment for those who say there’s a shortage.
Even so, he also said the U.S. has some systems “where it’s a little bit tighter, and we’re getting them in on a daily basis,” although he didn’t provide any details.
In his letter, Feinberg focused on needs beyond those related to the Iran war, including satellite communications and next-generation air-defense systems. Another priority is Lockheed Martin’s Next Generation Interceptor, a program aimed at defending the U.S. from intercontinental ballistic missiles. It’s a new warhead to replace the current ones used on U.S. missile interceptors in California and Alaska.
He asked companies to submit their plans by late August “for more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production capacity” in the critical programs he identified.
Feinberg’s memo outlined “critical programs under consideration for acceleration or increased procurement” during the upcoming fiscal 2028 defense plan that focus on naval and land-based radar designed to enhance missile defense capabilities rather than additional specific missiles used against Iran.
The programs he cited include:
—RTX’s naval AN/SPY-6 air and missile defense radar installed on the Navy’s latest DDG-51 destroyers
—Lockheed Martin’s land-based AN/TPY-6 radar, originally intended to provide 360-degree coverage of Guam from Chinese missiles
—RTX’s Lower Tier Air and Missile Defense Sensor, or LTAMDS, which is part of the air defense network guarding the US capital region
—Leidos Holdings Inc.’s Army Long-Range Persistent Surveillance radar network, which is starting to be deployed in the U.S. as part of the Golden Dome national missile defense network
—Boeing’s T-7A Red Hawk pilot training aircraft
—General Dynamics Corp.’s TAO-205 John Lewis class naval fleet refueling vessels
—Lockheed Martin’s Infrared Search and Track targeting pod for the F-15 fighter
—National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System, built by Kongsberg and RTX. The system has been supplied by the U.S. to Ukraine.
—RTX’s Advanced Extremely High Frequency Terminal, the ground-based link to the U.S. satellite constellation, providing jam-resistant communications to the military and national leadership
Feinberg asked industry leaders in their responses to outline the capital expenditures and facilities expenditures they will make to “support the department’s commitment to higher volume, sustained orders.”

sources.news_title: Pentagon pushes arms makers to boost output as Iran war drains stocks – WaPo
sources.text:
The Department of War has given defense contractors until late August to propose “significantly faster” delivery schedules, according to a memo seen by US media
The Pentagon is pressing US arms makers to accelerate production as the ongoing war with Iran depletes critical weapons stockpiles, the Washington Post reported on Saturday, citing a Department of War memo to industry leaders.
The memo, written by Deputy Secretary of War Steve Feinberg and reportedly sent earlier this week, gives manufacturers 21 days to propose “significantly faster” and “more aggressive” delivery schedules, expanded production capacity, or both.
“Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,” Feinberg wrote. “We must dramatically accelerate our program schedules and expand our production capacity now.”
The memo identifies several critical programs, including next-generation air-defense equipment, surface-to-air missile systems, satellite communications, and space-based missile tracking. Feinberg also called on industry leaders to propose investments and facility expansions to support “higher volume, sustained orders.”
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell confirmed to the media on Saturday that the memo is real and will help shape the fiscal 2028 budget, calling it “consistent with our ongoing push to rebuild the defense industrial base.”
While Parnell said the effort is part of a broader modernization drive predating the Iran war, it comes after months of fighting that have depleted already diminished US munitions stocks.
Read more
The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated last month that Patriot interceptor stocks fell from 2,330 before the war to 1,030 by the April ceasefire and now stand at 759 to 827 – down at least 65%. THAAD interceptors dropped from 452 to 234-278 – at least 38% below pre-war levels. The US also reportedly fired more than 1,300 Army tactical ballistic missiles during the initial weeks of fighting alone.
US President Donald Trump has vehemently denied any shortages, accusing the media of spreading misinformation. Earlier this week, he insisted on Truth Social that the US has “massive amounts” of weaponry. In later comments to reporters, he acknowledged that supplies of some unspecified systems are “a little bit tighter,” but maintained that stockpiles remain “literally massive,” with replacements arriving daily. Nevertheless, Trump reiterated that he would not give Patriots to Ukraine, which has long demanded more of the systems, saying “we want missiles too.”
The Pentagon has spent recent months trying to turn up the production dial. Last week, it announced a framework agreement with Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin to boost output of Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) and THAAD missiles. A similar deal has been agreed with RTX’s Raytheon to increase production of Tomahawk and several other missile systems. In May, the Pentagon also struck agreements with Anduril, Castelion, CoAspire, Leidos, and Zone 5 to expand strike capabilities and procure lower-cost missiles.
However, experts say the framework agreements are legally non-binding and hinge on congressional funding, specifically the proposed $1.15 trillion defense bill that remains deadlocked after Senate Democrats blocked it in mid-July, opposing the massive spending increase and Trump’s military action against Iran without congressional approval.
        
            READ MORE: Iran war leaves US allies in Asia less defended – NYT
        
    
US taxpayers also appear increasingly skeptical. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Tuesday found that just 35% of Americans approve of US military action in Iran, while other polls have indicated broad opposition to Iran war spending and the White House’s trillion-dollar-plus military budget.
US-Iran peace efforts remain stalled after a Pakistan-brokered interim agreement reached in mid-June quickly unraveled amid renewed skirmishes and tanker attacks, with both sides trading blame for violations.
On Saturday, Iran laid out new conditions for talks, demanding Washington lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, withdraw forces “from the area surrounding Iran,” remove “unjust and illegal” sanctions, release frozen Iranian assets, and pay compensation before negotiations can resume.

sources.text:
Pentagon urges faster US weapons production amid stockpile concerns
US defence industry pressed to boost output as munitions shortages raise security concerns amid Middle East tensions.
The Pentagon has called on the United States defence industry to accelerate production of weapons to help replenish its diminished stockpile of munitions, including those depleted in the ongoing war with Iran.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement on Saturday that the department was actively focused on boosting munitions acquisitions to provide “the weapons our warfighters need at the pace the threat demands”. He confirmed the department’s efforts over the last week to significantly speed up the process, but insisted it was part of a broader modernisation effort that predated the five-month-old conflict.

- list 2 of 3US officials push back on reports of dangerously low munitions supplies
- list 3 of 3Trump vows to find ‘leakers’ after reports of depleted Iran war munitions
Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg wrote to industry leaders on Wednesday, giving them no more than 21 days to submit plans to “drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities,” according to a memo obtained by The Washington Post.
“Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,” Feinberg wrote. “We must dramatically accelerate our program schedules and expand our production capacity now.”
The memo comes as recent fighting with Iran used up more of the US military’s already diminished stockpiles of advanced missile interceptors. Experts say shortages in both offensive and defensive weapons could leave US forces less secure.
Shrunken inventories of Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors may force the US and its Middle Eastern allies to take greater risks to conserve those air defences, according to an analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank. For example, it said, American forces may launch fewer missiles against incoming Iranian drones and missiles, raising the chance of one getting through.
US President Donald Trump has bristled over public reports of a munitions shortage. On Thursday, he again denied that the US faced any strategic disadvantage when it came to weapons stores after five months of war.
“The US has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social account. He added that “large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the US as needed” and that defence contractors are “building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history”.
On Saturday, Parnell affirmed that Feinberg’s memo seeking a rapid escalation of weapons production is “real,” adding that it “will inform the fiscal year 2028 budget submitted to Congress for funding, and it is entirely consistent with our ongoing push to rebuild the defense industrial base.”
A defence spending bill is currently stalled in the US Congress, with lawmakers fuming over Trump’s military action against Iran and resisting the White House request to substantially increase Pentagon spending to $1.5 trillion, up from about $900bn last year. Experts have warned that even with an influx of funding, it will likely take at least three years to restore Patriot and THAAD interceptors to pre-war levels.
The number of Patriot interceptors fell from 2,330 before the war to 1,030 when the April ceasefire took effect, CSIS estimated last month. Following recent fighting, the stockpile is now estimated to be between 759 and 827, a decrease of at least 65 percent since before the conflict began.
The number of THAAD interceptors fell from 452 before the war to between 232 and 262 at the start of the April ceasefire, CSIS said. The US was able to replenish some of the inventory to between 234 and 278 interceptors. But the stockpile is still at least 38 percent smaller than it was before the conflict.
Earlier this month, the US Department of Defense penned a new deal with defence giants Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman in an effort to ramp up production capacity for parts used in missile defence systems.
“We don’t have that many [interceptors] left, and there are no good substitutes,” retired US Marine Corps colonel Mark Cancian, one of the authors of the CSIS analysis, told Al Jazeera on Wednesday. “If we run out of Patriots, then the missiles get through.”

sources.news_title: Pentagon races to rebuild weapons stockpile as Iran war drains supplies
sources.text:
The Pentagon is pressing major U.S. defense contractors to accelerate weapons production, issuing strict deadlines to replenish critical military stockpiles depleted during the conflict with Iran, according to newly disclosed Defense Department directives.
Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg wrote to industry leaders on Wednesday, giving them no more than 21 days to submit plans to drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities, according to a memo obtained by The Washington Post.
“Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,” Feinberg wrote in the memo, demanding faster program schedules and an expansion of production capacity.
In a statement to Newsweek on Sunday morning, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that from day one under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, "this Department has been focused on delivering generational change to the speed, capacity, and lethality of America’s defense industrial base and the Arsenal of Freedom."
He continued: "Deputy Secretary Feinberg is a generational leader in that effort, driving the hard work of fixing our broken, antiquated, and immensely complex acquisitions system so we can actually produce the weapons our warfighters need at the pace the threat demands. Working directly with industry leaders to accelerate production is not new. It has been the clear intent of the President and this Secretary from the start."
Concerns Over Depleted Missile Defenses
The initiative underscores mounting concern within military planning circles that months of combat against Iran have significantly reduced inventories of key missile defense systems, such as Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors. Shrunken inventories of these interceptors may force the U.S. and its Middle Eastern allies to take more risks to conserve those air defenses, according to an analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a Washington think tank. American forces may launch fewer missiles against incoming Iranian drones and missiles, raising the chance of one getting through.
According to the CSIS analysis, the number of Patriot interceptors fell from 2,330 before the Iran war to 1,030 when the April ceasefire took effect, and following recent fighting, the stockpile is now estimated to be between 759 and 827—a decrease of at least 65 percent since before the conflict began. Similarly, the number of THAAD interceptors fell from 452 before the war to between 232 and 262 at the start of the April ceasefire; while the U.S. was able to partially replenish the inventory to between 234 and 278 interceptors, the stockpile remains at least 38 percent smaller than it was before the conflict.
Restocking heavily depleted items—such as Patriot, THAAD, and Tomahawk cruise missiles—could take at least three years, even with elevated funding.
Costs and Administration Pushback
Hegseth informed senators last month that the war with Iran has cost an estimated $37.5 billion since hostilities began in late February, covering current operations and projected needs through the end of the fiscal year on September 30.
While President Donald Trump pushed back on reports of critical shortages, stating on Truth Social on Thursday that the United States maintains “massive amounts” of weaponry and that “large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed,” Pentagon officials maintain that the production push is essential to fortifying the broader defense industrial base. On Saturday, Parnell affirmed that Feinberg's memo is “real,” adding that it “will inform the fiscal year 2028 budget submitted to Congress for funding.”
Meanwhile, a defense spending bill is currently stalled in Congress, with lawmakers fuming over Trump’s military action against Iran and resisting the White House request to substantially increase Pentagon spending to $1.5 trillion, up from about $900 billion last year.
Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Steve Mollman and Anthony Murray.

sources.news_title: Trump denies critical weapons shortage - but US allies are paying the price
sources.text:
Donald Trump has denied reports that the US is running low on critical weapons systems as a result of the war with Iran – but nations around the world are struggling to protect their skies as air defence interceptor stocks run down.
The US military has largely exhausted stockpiles of advanced long-range munitions such as the ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles, The New York Times reported on Sunday, citing senior US officials.
Stocks of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) air defence interceptors have been reduced by up to 80 per cent, CNN reported this week. Military commanders told the US network that supplies were “dangerously low”.
The Pentagon has also burned through two thirds of Patriot air defence missiles, according to analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
The think tank described Operation Epic Fury – the military campaign against Iran – as Washington’s “most munitions-intensive military campaign in decades.”
It added: “The conflict has consumed thousands of advanced offensive and defensive missiles, placing unprecedented strain on inventories of critical systems such as Patriot interceptors, THAAD interceptors, Tomahawk cruise missiles, and other high-end precision munitions.
“Questions about the depth of US stockpiles, production capacity, and military readiness have become central to national security planning.”
Trump and his top officials have fiercely denied shortages. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said the military had “more than enough firepower to carry out any operation the President orders at any time and place”. Trump has threatened to jail anyone leaking information about weapons.
But the White House is pressing defence companies to rapidly scale up production of a range of critical systems including Patriot and THAAD interceptors.
An internal memo from deputy defence secretary Steve Feinberg, first reported by The Washington Post and confirmed to be legitimate by the Pentagon, called on industry chiefs to “drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities”, warning that “years-long development cycles are not acceptable”.
The current timelines to replace Patriot and THAAD munitions are more than four years, according to CSIS.
Shortages are being felt far beyond the US, which supplies Patriot systems and munitions to many of its allies.
Gulf countries have reportedly expended around 800 Patriot interceptors to defend against Iranian missile strikes in recent months, which they are struggling to replace.
Ukraine is searching desperately for air defence ammunition that allies are struggling to supply. The Pentagon has failed to fulfil pre-existing Patriot orders to European countries such as Switzerland, which is now exploring alternatives.
Even before the Iran war, demand for Patriot missiles, which can be used against aircraft and cruise and ballistic missiles, was already outstripping supply.
Justin Bronk, Senior Research Fellow in Airpower and Technology at defence think-tank Rusi, said: “Public figures for global production of Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles generally sit between 600 and 700 per year. There was a greater demand than that from global Patriot users including particularly Ukraine, Saudi Arabia and the UAE prior to Operation Epic Fury.”
Other types of air defence systems cannot easily plug the gaps. “Larger, more capable interceptors such as THAAD and SM-6/SM-3 were produced in far smaller numbers than PAC-3 MSE [an interceptor built for the Patriot system] and have also been used in very large numbers relative to available stocks since the first large Israeli-Iranian exchanges in 2024.”
European missile stockpiles have also been depleted since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with allies donating air defences to Kyiv. Without a rapid increase in production, the shortages may leave European skies exposed.
Lami Kim, a defence expert at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) wrote that stockpiles have been “markedly reduced”.
Some western and central European countries – including Germany, the Netherlands, Romania and Spain – transferred US-supplied Patriot systems to Ukraine following the outbreak of war. This shortage has been exacerbated by many eastern European countries seeking to phase out legacy Soviet-era systems, Kim added.
“Against this backdrop, air and missile defence was among the seven critical capability areas identified as requiring urgent action to close existing gaps in the 2025 White Paper for European Defence – Readiness 2030,” she wrote, describing the shortfall in European medium and long-range ballistic missile defence as “acute”.
“Europe has relied mainly on the US-made Patriot system. Germany has purchased the Arrow 3 long-range air-defence system, developed by Israel Aerospace Industries with Boeing as a co-developer and co-producer, but this represents only a small fraction of the air and missile defence capacity Europe needs.”
Even when the supply of interceptors increases, Europe may not be prioritised for buying them. “Under such conditions, the US is likely to prioritise replenishing its own stocks before fulfilling external demand,” Kim said. “When exports do resume, its Gulf partners may take precedence. Europe could be near the end of the queue.”
In Ukraine, shortages are being felt daily, with Russia exploiting gaps in air defences with devastating barrages. Matthew Arnold, director of LSE Ideas’ Democratic Resilience in a New Age of War Programme, recently told The i Paper: “In Kyiv, there just haven’t been the Patriots to respond,” with Russia “maximising the ballistics because they know Ukraine is in a miserable spot right now”.
Ukrainian air defence commanders told The New York Times that Ukrainian forces had adapted their tactics to try to preserve interceptor missiles, switching units to manual mode so they fire one missile at a time, rather than the standard two or three.
To plug the gap, Ukraine is set to be the first country to receive two of the next-generation Franco-Italian SAMP/T NG air defence systems in October. Trump has said he will grant Ukraine a licence to produce its own Patriot missiles, but appeared to backtrack this month.
Even if a licence is granted, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said domestic Patriot production could take years to deliver the vital munitions. Domestic company Fire Point is aiming to roll out its own anti-ballistic system, but this too could involve a timeline of years.
Russian analysts see a window of opportunity emerging. “The less precision-guided weaponry the US has, the less will reach Ukraine,” said military blogger Alexander Kots.
Europe is scrambling to expand its own defence industries, to shore up sovereign supply chains of critical military capabilities. In this year’s Defence Investment Plan, the UK committed £790m to “enhance protection of the UK homeland and overseas bases from air, drone and missile threats over the next four years”.
But for now, air and missile defence remains a serious concern for militaries around the world – whatever Trump might say.

The Pentagon is directing weapons manufacturers to propose sharply faster production schedules as estimates show major declines in Patriot and THAAD interceptor inventories following months of fighting with Iran.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
The Pentagon is pressing U.S. defense contractors to rapidly expand weapons production as the military works to replenish munitions inventories that have been reduced by months of conflict, including substantial use of advanced missile interceptors during fighting with Iran.
Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg gave defense industry leaders no more than 21 days to submit proposals outlining how they can deliver critical weapons faster and increase manufacturing capacity, according to a Wednesday memo obtained by The Washington Post.
The directive calls on companies to “drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities.”
“Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,” Feinberg wrote. “We must dramatically accelerate our program schedules and expand our production capacity now.”
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell confirmed Saturday that the department has intensified its efforts during the past week to speed weapons procurement and production. He said the objective is to provide “the weapons our warfighters need at the pace the threat demands.”
Parnell characterized the initiative as part of a wider effort to modernize weapons procurement and rebuild U.S. manufacturing capacity rather than a policy created solely in response to the five-month-old conflict with Iran.
The renewed production push comes as estimates indicate that U.S. supplies of some of its most advanced air-defense interceptors have fallen considerably.
A recent analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies found that the fighting with Iran consumed additional quantities from already diminished inventories of Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, interceptors.
The Washington-based think tank warned that lower stockpiles could force the United States and its allies in the Middle East to make more difficult decisions about when to use their remaining air-defense missiles if fighting resumes.
One possible consequence, according to the analysis, is that U.S. forces could fire fewer interceptors against incoming Iranian missiles and drones in an attempt to preserve supplies. Doing so could increase the likelihood that an incoming weapon penetrates American air defenses.
The estimated decline has drawn public attention even as President Donald Trump has rejected reports suggesting the United States faces a shortage.
Trump wrote Thursday on Truth Social that the country possesses “massive amounts” of munitions and said “large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed.”
Parnell on Saturday confirmed that Feinberg’s directive to defense manufacturers is “real,” while emphasizing that the initiative extends beyond immediate battlefield requirements.
The memo “will inform the fiscal year 2028 budget submitted to Congress for funding, and it is entirely consistent with our ongoing push to rebuild the defense industrial base,” Parnell said.
The Pentagon’s effort is unfolding while a defense spending measure remains stalled in Congress. Lawmakers have expressed anger over Trump’s military actions against Iran, while some are also resisting a White House request to raise Pentagon spending substantially.
The administration is seeking approximately $1.5 trillion in defense spending, compared with about $900 billion last year.
Estimates of Patriot interceptor inventories illustrate the scale of the depletion cited by analysts.
CSIS estimated last month that the United States had approximately 2,330 Patriot interceptors before the war. By the time an April ceasefire took effect, that figure had fallen to roughly 1,030.
Following more recent fighting, the estimated inventory declined further to between 759 and 827 Patriot interceptors. That represents a reduction of at least 65% from the level estimated before the conflict began.
THAAD inventories have also declined.
According to CSIS, the United States possessed approximately 452 THAAD interceptors before the war. The number had dropped to between 232 and 262 by the beginning of the April ceasefire.
Some of those losses were subsequently replenished, bringing the estimated inventory to between 234 and 278 interceptors. Even after that replenishment, however, the THAAD stockpile remains at least 38% below its estimated prewar level.
The Pentagon is now seeking production plans from manufacturers that could shorten delivery timelines and expand output of critical systems as officials prepare future defense budgets and attempt to rebuild inventories consumed during recent military operations.

US military pushes companies to ‘dramatically accelerate’ weapons production as Iran war burns through supply, memo says
The munitions shortage reportedly prompted President Trump to chew out Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last at Camp David
With the Iran war draining U.S. weapons stockpiles, the Pentagon is reportedly leaning hard on defense companies to bump up production — and fast.
In a memo on Wednesday, Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg gave companies three weeks to lay out how they would “drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities.”
“Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,” Feinberg added in the memo, which was obtained by The Washington Post. “We must dramatically accelerate our program schedules and expand our production capacity now.”
The Pentagon confirmed the existence of the August 5 memo and praised Feinberg as a “generational leader” who was “fixing our broken, antiquated, and immensely complex acquisitions system.”
“Working directly with industry leaders to accelerate production is not new,” chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell wrote in a statement to The Independent. “It has been the clear intent of the President and this Secretary from the start.”
“The fiscal year 2027 budget currently being considered on Capitol Hill could supercharge this effort today,” he added.
The demands come after weapons manufacturers were reportedly summoned to the White House in July, where they were allegedly urged to lobby Congress to pass another round of funding.
President Donald Trump has insisted the U.S. still has “massive amounts” of weapons, though tempers have reportedly flared over the issue behind the scenes.
The president reportedly confronted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at Camp David last week over the munitions shortage, claiming he thought the problem “had been fixed” already.
The Trump administration has denied this account, while the president has threatened jail time for the “treasonous” leakers that fueled the reporting.

The military has also burned through roughly half of its Patriot interceptors and nearly four-fifths of its Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missile inventory compared to pre-war levels, CNN reported.
The Iran conflict has been something of a strategic mismatch. Tehran, despite possessing a much smaller military than the U.S., has pummeled American bases across the Middle East with low-cost, single-use drones, which the U.S. often has to use expensive interceptors to stop.
The U.S. military had 2,330 Patriot systems and 452 THAAD systems before the war, according to a July report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

sources.news_title: Pentagon warns arms makers to accelerate output as U.S. munitions crisis grows
sources.text:
The war with Iran continues to rapidly erode the United States’ stockpile of missiles and interceptors, and the Pentagon is now increasing pressure on defense contractors to expand factories and dramatically accelerate production. In a memo obtained by The Washington Post and published overnight Saturday into Sunday, weapons manufacturers were ordered to present, within 21 days, plans for faster supply and expanded production capacity for weapons systems defined as critical.
The memo was sent Wednesday by Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg, who made clear to the industry that development processes that take years no longer match the needs of the U.S. military. According to him, the Pentagon wants to fundamentally change the way it develops, produces and fields military capabilities, and move to a model that allows production at a pace suited to a prolonged war. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell confirmed to the Post that the memo is authentic, and said its conclusions would also be used in shaping the defense budget for fiscal 2028.
The reason for the pressure becomes clear when looking at the pace of weapons use since the start of the war. In the first month alone, the U.S. fired more than 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles and more than 1,000 Patriot and THAAD interceptors. In the first weeks of fighting, the U.S. military also used more than 1,300 tactical ballistic missiles from the Army.
According to an assessment by the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, the U.S. stockpile of Patriot interceptors worldwide fell from about 2,200 on the eve of the war to fewer than 827 by the end of last month. The stockpile of THAAD interceptors, whose role is to intercept ballistic missiles at high altitude, fell from about 452 to fewer than 278. Another analysis by the institute found that the U.S. had already used about 65% of the Patriot interceptors it had at the start of the war, while the THAAD stockpile fell by at least 38%.
The erosion is not limited to defense systems. Reuters reported last week that over five months of fighting, the U.S. military used “almost all” of its global stockpile of long-range precision ATACMS and PrSM missiles. One source who spoke with the agency estimated that the U.S. had also used slightly less than half of its Tomahawk stockpile. Administration officials have therefore expressed concern that continued use at the current pace would damage the American ability to deal with another crisis elsewhere in the world, particularly a war scenario involving China or Russia.
The figure that perhaps best illustrates the scale of the challenge is the production rate for the Tomahawk. While more than 850 missiles of that type were fired in just one month of the war, the production rate for the U.S. military has until now stood at only about 60 missiles a year. Under a multiyear agreement with RTX, Raytheon’s parent company, the Pentagon plans to gradually raise production capacity to 1,000 Tomahawks a year — more than 16 times the current rate.
Unusual steps are also being taken with interceptors. Last week, the Army awarded Lockheed Martin a contract worth up to $58.6 billion to produce PAC-3 MSE interceptors for the Patriot system. The company plans to triple production capacity by 2030 and increase the workforce at its plant in Camden, Arkansas, by 50%. In addition, the Pentagon announced a framework agreement worth more than $3 billion with Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman, intended to allow production capacity for Patriot components to be tripled and THAAD component production to be quadrupled.
The problem is not only the number of missiles ordered. Production depends on complex supply chains and a limited number of factories and suppliers, so under the agreement the Pentagon plans, among other things, to establish a second production source for the solid rocket motors of PAC-3 interceptors and expand production of other critical components. In doing so, Washington is trying to reduce bottlenecks that could delay increasing the pace even if billions of additional dollars are injected into the industry.
The Pentagon to industry: Invest your own money, too
One of the unusual parts of the new memo concerns what the Pentagon is demanding from the companies themselves. Feinberg asked manufacturers to detail which capital investments they are prepared to make and which factories can be expanded to support large orders over time. In effect, he is demanding that they assume part of the risk and invest their own money even before Congress has guaranteed full funding for future orders.
Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project at Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), told the Post that some companies have already begun funding parts of their production expansion themselves, but from their perspective it is a gamble: These are publicly traded companies spending large sums based on a promise that the administration will later order large quantities of weapons from them. Such a promise, however, ultimately also depends on Congress.
And that is precisely one of the main obstacles in the plan. In recent months, the Pentagon has announced a series of “framework agreements” with weapons manufacturers, but those are not binding contracts to purchase the munitions. Turning them into actual orders requires money Congress has not yet approved. According to The Washington Post, a defense budget proposal totaling about $1.15 trillion remains stuck in Congress amid the dispute over the scope of spending.
The situation led the White House to take another unusual step. In late July, senior executives from Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman and Boeing were summoned there, alongside next-generation companies Anduril and Palantir. They met with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Office of Management and Budget director Russell Vought and White House congressional affairs director James Braid. According to three sources who spoke with the Post, the company executives were asked to personally approach lawmakers and pressure them to approve an increase in defense spending.
At the same time, the Pentagon is trying to break its dependence on the veteran weapons giants and bring younger technology companies into the picture. In May, framework agreements were signed with Anduril, Castelion, CoAspire, Leidos and Zone 5 in an effort to buy large quantities of relatively low-cost missiles and quickly expand U.S. strike capabilities. The administration also recruited senior figures from Silicon Valley, including Emil Michael, a former senior Uber executive who was appointed undersecretary of defense for research and engineering as part of the effort to change the Pentagon’s procurement and development system.
Feinberg’s memo also identifies a series of systems whose purchase or development the Pentagon is considering accelerating as part of the 2028 budget. They include the next-generation interceptor for ballistic missile defense, the NASAMS air defense system, a mobile air defense radar, an advanced pilot training system and a space-based missile tracking system.
Even if the war stops, refilling the warehouses will take years
But even a dramatic acceleration of production will not solve the problem quickly. According to a CSIS analysis, at the expected delivery pace, it would take three years or more to restore Tomahawk, Patriot and THAAD inventories to their prewar levels. Restoring stocks of SM-3 and SM-6 missiles is expected to take about two years, while in the case of JASSM and PrSM missiles, it would take months to about a year.
With the Tomahawk, for example, the problem stems not only from production capacity, but also from the long delivery time. The Navy requested the purchase of 785 additional missiles as part of the 2027 budget, but under the current forecast the first of them will not reach operational stocks until March 2030 because of a production time of nearly three years. According to CSIS, only toward the end of 2030 is the U.S. expected to replenish the number of Tomahawks fired in the war.
There is also additional pressure on the production lines: The U.S. does not manufacture missiles only for itself. It must simultaneously meet commitments to its allies, including Ukraine, Japan, Australia and European countries. CSIS warned that demand exceeding supply is already causing friction over the question of who will receive the new munitions first. Japan, for example, is supposed to receive hundreds of Tomahawk missiles, but delivery could be delayed if the Pentagon decides to prioritize replenishing American stocks.
Beyond the current war, Washington is especially concerned about the implications for a possible confrontation in the western Pacific. CSIS warned that the erosion has created a “window of vulnerability” in terms of preparedness for war with China. The shortage of Patriot and THAAD interceptors may also force U.S. forces and their allies to take greater risks in deciding which Iranian missiles to intercept and which not to, because there is currently no full substitute for those systems against ballistic missiles.
The shortage has also become a political issue within the Trump administration. According to reports, senior military officials warned for weeks that interceptor stocks were shrinking, and concern over continued erosion was among the considerations presented to the president against launching another massive attack in Iran. Reuters reported that the shortage of long-range missiles could even force the U.S. to rely more on fighter jets and crewed bombers, and take greater risks to hit targets that could otherwise have been attacked from a distance using precision missiles.
The inventory crisis has also become a focus of tension inside the Trump administration in recent days. According to a report a few days ago in The Washington Post, the president confronted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at Camp David and demanded to know why he had been presented, according to him, with a picture suggesting that the munitions problem had already been dealt with. Trump himself rejected claims that the U.S. was approaching a dangerous point, writing Thursday that his country has “massive” quantities of munitions and that additional weapons are being produced and sent to it as needed. The Pentagon also insists that the military has all the capabilities it needs to carry out its missions.

US Pentagon asks defence firms to boost production of key systems amid concerns over shortage
WASHINGTON – The Pentagon’s No. 2 official has asked major US defence companies to accelerate efforts to produce and deliver key weapons systems amid new concerns about shortages and gaps exacerbated by the Iran war.
Steve Feinberg, the deputy secretary of defence, said the department is targeting accelerated or increased procurement for critical programmes including wide-area surveillance, air-defence sensors and interceptors, and missile-tracking systems.
“Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,” he wrote in an Aug 5 letter seen by Bloomberg to major defence companies, including Boeing, Lockheed Martin and RTX.
“We must dramatically accelerate our programme schedules and expand our production capacity now.” The Washington Post reported earlier on the letter.
There have been growing warnings about the state of US weapons stockpiles as the US military attacks Iran and repels its drone and missile strikes on American bases in the region.
US President Donald Trump has denied the US is running low on munitions, saying on Aug 6 the country has “massive amounts” of them, while threatening to punish those who say there is a shortage.
But he also said the US has some systems “where it’s a little bit tighter and we’re getting them in on a daily basis”, although he did not give details.
In his letter, Feinberg focused on needs beyond those related to the Iran war, including satellite communications and next-generation air-defence systems. Another priority is Lockheed Martin’s Next Generation Interceptor, a programme aimed at defending the US from intercontinental ballistic missiles.
He asked companies to submit their plans by late August “for more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production capacity” in the critical programmes that he identified. BLOOMBERG

The unanswered question is how much of the coming Pentagon spending Michigan can capture.
Iran War Creates A Manufacturing Problem
The scale of America’s munitions problem became increasingly apparent during the Iran war.
Reuters reported Aug. 4 that the United States had used virtually all of some categories of long-range precision missiles available for the conflict, adding to concerns about inventories of other sophisticated weapons, including Patriot and THAAD air-defense interceptors and Tomahawk cruise missiles.
The Pentagon is now pushing defense manufacturers to rapidly increase production.
The Defense Department has instructed defense companies to develop plans for accelerating production of critical weapons, while billions of dollars are beginning to flow into expanded missile-manufacturing capacity.
Recent agreements worth more than $3 billion are aimed at expanding production of critical components used in Patriot and THAAD interceptors. Pentagon plans call for substantially increasing production of both systems.
The military also wants a dramatic increase in production of Tomahawk cruise missiles.
But modern weapons cannot simply be replaced by adding another shift to an assembly plant.
Missiles contain sophisticated electronics, guidance systems, sensors, propulsion systems and specialized materials produced by networks of contractors and subcontractors.
Some weapons require years to replenish in significant quantities.
That turns America’s ability to manufacture weapons into a national-security issue — and potentially an economic opportunity for states capable of producing them.
GM Sees Defense As A Growth Business
General Motors is already moving deeper into defense.
CEO Mary Barra identified GM Defense during GM’s July earnings report as one of the company’s growth businesses creating additional opportunities outside its traditional automotive operations.
GM Defense is expected to generate approximately $700 million in revenue this year — still small compared with GM’s enormous automotive business but increasingly significant as Washington searches for ways to expand America’s defense industrial base.
More importantly, GM is developing relationships with major defense contractors.
In June, GM Defense and Lockheed Martin announced an agreement to explore combining Lockheed Martin’s defense expertise with GM’s commercial manufacturing capabilities.
Among the objectives is strengthening defense supply chains and potentially expanding defense production capacity by applying GM’s high-volume manufacturing expertise.
GM Defense reportedly also has discussed potential cooperation with other major defense contractors.
GM doesn’t necessarily have to design the next Patriot missile.
Its potential value to the Pentagon may be something Detroit has understood for more than a century: how to manufacture complicated products at enormous scale.
That expertise could also create opportunities throughout GM’s Michigan supplier network.
Ford Is Moving Back Into Defense Too
Ford Motor Co. also sees an opportunity.
Governments in North America and Europe have approached Ford about supporting modern defense requirements, and the Dearborn automaker has publicly argued that its commercial vehicles, software, engineering and mass-manufacturing capabilities could help military customers deploy equipment more quickly and at lower cost.
Ford also has entered the competition to build the U.S. Army’s next heavy infantry tactical vehicle.
Its prototype for the Infantry Squad Vehicle-Heavy program will draw on Ford’s F-Series Super Duty platform.
The Army competition represents one of Ford’s most significant moves back into military vehicles since the company sold Ford Aerospace decades ago.
Ford has summed up its defense proposition in four words:
“Speed, scale, capability, and durability.”
Those same capabilities exist throughout Michigan’s automotive supply chain.
Could Auto Suppliers Become Defense Suppliers?
That could be where the largest Michigan employment opportunity emerges.
Michigan doesn’t necessarily need to become the place where Patriot, THAAD or Tomahawk missiles are assembled.
Those weapons already have established prime contractors and manufacturing locations.
But dramatically increasing production requires far more than expanding final assembly.
Missiles, drones, military vehicles and aerospace systems require thousands of components produced throughout extensive supply chains.
Those include electronics, sensors, precision-machined parts, castings, propulsion components, batteries, advanced materials, software, tooling and manufacturing equipment.
Michigan companies already produce many of those technologies for automotive, mobility and advanced manufacturing.
Some are already Pentagon suppliers.
Thousands of others potentially possess manufacturing capabilities that could be adapted to defense work.
For Michigan workers, that could translate into demand for engineers, software developers, artificial-intelligence specialists, machinists, electricians, technicians and other skilled manufacturing workers.
It also could provide Michigan automotive suppliers with another market at a time when electrification, automation and changing vehicle technology are disrupting traditional auto-industry business models.
So far, MITechNews has found no publicly announced Pentagon contract awarded specifically to a Michigan company to replenish weapons expended during the Iran war.
But the Pentagon’s production expansion is only beginning.
As major defense contractors increase output, they may need additional suppliers — and Michigan wants to be one of the places they look.
The Next Arsenal May Be Built Around Cheap Drones
There is another possibility: rebuilding America’s arsenal may not mean replacing every expensive weapon expended during the Iran war with another identical weapon.
Lessons from Ukraine and now Iran are accelerating military interest in what defense planners call “affordable mass” — producing large numbers of relatively inexpensive drones and autonomous weapons that can perform some missions now assigned to much more costly systems.
The Army is pursuing plans to acquire hundreds of thousands of small unmanned aircraft, including inexpensive one-way attack drones. The Pentagon also is examining cheaper unmanned systems capable of performing some missions currently handled by aircraft costing millions of dollars.
Cheap drones cannot replace Patriot and THAAD interceptors or sophisticated long-range missiles across the battlefield. Those systems provide speed, range, defensive capabilities and destructive power that small drones cannot duplicate.
But the economics of warfare are changing.
Using weapons costing millions of dollars against every lower-cost target can become difficult to sustain during a prolonged conflict. Thousands of inexpensive drones could handle some surveillance, reconnaissance and strike missions while allowing the military to reserve its most sophisticated weapons for targets that actually require them.
That could play directly to Michigan’s strengths — and potentially create an entirely new manufacturing sector.
The state’s defense strategy specifically identifies drones and unmanned systems as an industry Michigan wants to expand.
Many of the technologies needed to build autonomous systems already exist within Michigan’s automotive and mobility industries: electric motors, batteries, power electronics, sensors, cameras, communications systems, artificial intelligence, autonomous-driving software and high-volume manufacturing.
Michigan’s original Arsenal of Democracy was built around mass production.
The next one may be too.
Except instead of only tanks, trucks and bombers, Michigan factories could someday mass-produce drones, autonomous vehicles and AI-powered military systems.
Michigan Launches Five-Year Defense Expansion
The timing is striking.
Michigan has just released its Michigan Defense and Aerospace Strategic Plan 2026-2031, a five-year effort to expand the state’s defense industrial base.
The Michigan Office of Defense and Aerospace Innovation estimates Michigan’s defense economy generates approximately $30 billion in economic activity and supports more than 166,000 jobs.
The state has more than 4,000 defense-aligned companies and approximately 900 aerospace suppliers.
Michigan’s traditional military strength remains ground vehicles.
The Detroit Arsenal in Warren is home to the U.S. Army Tank-automotive and Armaments Command and the Army’s Ground Vehicle Systems Center, making Southeast Michigan one of the centers of U.S. military ground-vehicle research and procurement.
But Michigan’s new strategy aims considerably higher.
The state identifies growth opportunities involving drones and unmanned systems, artificial intelligence, aerospace, advanced aerial mobility, space technologies, cybersecurity, maritime technologies and advanced energy systems.
It also calls for strengthening Michigan’s defense supply chain and helping companies move technologies from prototypes into full-scale production.
The state’s theme for the effort is particularly appropriate:
“Reimagining the Arsenal of Democracy.”
Michigan Already Has A Defense Industrial Base
Michigan isn’t starting from scratch.
The state is home to General Dynamics Land Systems in Sterling Heights and numerous companies producing military vehicles, transmissions, vehicle systems, armor, electronics and other defense-related products.
Michigan also possesses major military and testing assets including Selfridge Air National Guard Base, Camp Grayling and the National All-Domain Warfighting Center.
The state has 13 of the nation’s APEX Accelerators, which help companies navigate government contracting and compete for federal business.
Patrick Anderson, CEO of the Anderson Economic Group, told MITechNews following the Iran war that depleted weapons inventories will generate additional demand.
“The depletion of munitions and the wartime strain on defense assets means there will be new demand for replacing them,” Anderson said. “Much of that work can be done in the region that was once the ‘arsenal of democracy’ in WWII.”
Anderson said America’s World War II mobilization illustrates how broadly military spending can spread through an industrial economy.
Factories weren’t simply producing tanks and bombers. They needed engines, components, tooling, clothing, containers and thousands of other products supporting a military at war.
Today’s defense industry is very different and the scale of any industrial conversion would be considerably smaller.
But the supply-chain principle remains.
“Because Michigan is still the home of so much manufacturing, I think our state will get more of that business than most states,” Anderson said.
Michigan Has Plenty Of Competition
Winning that business won’t be automatic.
Michigan’s own strategic plan acknowledges weaknesses including fragmentation within the state’s defense ecosystem, inconsistent incentives and limited national recognition compared with states possessing large aerospace and military clusters.
Michigan also faces aggressive competition from states including Ohio, Alabama and Pennsylvania.
Those states want the same factories, Pentagon contracts and highly paid engineering and manufacturing jobs.
Michigan’s enormous automotive supply chain could provide an advantage — particularly if GM and Ford demonstrate that commercial automotive manufacturing can be successfully adapted to defense production.
But that advantage still has to be converted into contracts.
Workers Could Become The Next Shortage
Ironically, Michigan could win new defense investment and then confront another problem: finding enough workers.
A defense-industry workforce study released this summer found widespread difficulty recruiting people with skills required for advanced defense manufacturing.
Artificial intelligence, engineering, cybersecurity, skilled trades and advanced manufacturing are increasingly competing for limited pools of specialized workers.
That could make workforce development as important as economic-development incentives.
Michigan may possess the factories, suppliers and engineering heritage necessary to participate in a defense manufacturing boom but struggle to find enough workers to expand production.
The state’s defense strategy consequently identifies talent development as one of its priorities.
Iran Isn’t The Only Concern — There’s China
The national-security stakes extend beyond replacing weapons expended against Iran.
Military planners have warned that a conflict with China, particularly over Taiwan, could consume enormous quantities of precision-guided missiles, air-defense interceptors, drones and other sophisticated weapons in a matter of weeks.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies has warned that rebuilding U.S. missile inventories is a multiyear undertaking.
That leaves Washington confronting two problems simultaneously: replacing weapons already used while maintaining enough inventory to deter — or potentially fight — another major adversary.
The Iran war has demonstrated how quickly sophisticated weapons can be consumed.
The question now is whether America’s industrial base can manufacture replacements quickly enough.
Another Customer For Michigan
During World War II, Detroit’s automobile industry became America’s Arsenal of Democracy, turning automotive factories and suppliers toward production of tanks, trucks, engines and aircraft.
No comparable conversion of America’s civilian economy is being contemplated today.
Modern weapons are vastly more complex, defense contracting requirements are more demanding and America’s economy is fundamentally different from what it was in 1941.
But the underlying industrial question sounds familiar.
Does America possess enough factories, engineers, workers and suppliers to produce military equipment as quickly as modern warfare consumes it?
GM and Ford appear to see an opportunity in solving that problem.
Michigan does too.
Billions of dollars are beginning to flow toward rebuilding America’s depleted weapons inventories and expanding the defense industrial base.
So far, MITechNews has found no publicly announced Iran-war replenishment contract that has landed directly with a Michigan company.
But the competition for that money is only beginning.
And Michigan’s biggest opportunity may extend beyond helping traditional defense contractors build more expensive missiles.
It could involve taking technologies developed for automobiles — batteries, sensors, electric motors, artificial intelligence, autonomy and high-volume manufacturing — and applying them to a new generation of drones and military systems designed to be produced quickly and affordably.
Nearly 85 years after Michigan helped arm America for World War II, the state has another opportunity to compete for a larger role in America’s defense industry.
For Michigan’s changing automotive manufacturing economy, that could mean billions of dollars in new business.
And for Michigan workers, it could mean something even more important:
JOBS.

Washington: Amid concerns over shortages of key weapons following the war with Iran, the US Department of Defense has reportedly asked defence contractors to urgently increase weapons production and speed up deliveries.
According to The Washington Post, Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg met defence industry leaders on Wednesday and gave companies 21 days to submit plans to expand or significantly accelerate production of critical defence capabilities.
